_comment: Permission rules the plugin REQUIRES for the §3.7 single-permission contract to function. A plugin's own settings.json `permissions` block is silently ignored by the host, so these rules cannot ship as plugin defaults: /lua-doctor offers to merge this file into the user's project `.claude/settings.json` on first run, the user accepts once, and the rules persist for the project. Without them the plugin still works, but every safe `lua` call asks, and in a non-interactive session an ask is a refusal. Every command shape here is verified against lua-cli 3.58.0's src/cli/command-definitions.ts and src/utils/aliases.ts. Precedence is deny → ask → allow. HOW THE PRODUCTION GATE WORKS: the bare production verbs (`lua deploy …`, `lua version promote …`, `lua skills deploy …`, `lua mcp activate …`, `lua marketplace template publish …`, …) are deliberately in NEITHER deny NOR ask. A deny or ask rule matches past any leading assignment, so `Bash(lua deploy*)` in deny would also match the user-confirmed `LUA_DEPLOY_CONFIRMED=1 lua deploy …` form and make every deploy impossible — this template used to carry exactly that rule. The gate for the bare forms is hooks/confirm-deploy.mjs, whose block wins over any allow rule, including a broad `Bash(lua *)` in the user's own settings; it classifies with lib/tokenizer.mjs, which is the single source of truth for 'what changes production'. The `allow` rows below are the literal prefixed forms the deploy flow emits after the single confirmation, so a confirmed deploy runs without a second prompt. test/lib/permissions-mirror.test.mjs fails if any deny or ask rule would shadow a confirmed form, or if any allow rule admits a bare one. CREDENTIALS NEVER RIDE AN ALLOW RULE: `lua auth key` prints the raw API key to stdout and `lua auth configure` collects an email and a one-time code, so both are denied and belong in the user's own terminal; `lua auth logout` is denied because it discards a credential nothing here can restore. lua-cli installs the SAME program under three names (`lua`, `heylua`, `lua-ai` — its package.json `bin` block), so the alternatives are denied wholesale: a rule written only for `lua` left `heylua auth key` reachable. The plugin only ever emits `lua`. scripts/lint-permissions.mjs fails the build if any of that regresses. PER-VERB SPELLING MATTERS throughout: a blanket `Bash(lua decisions *)` in allow would admit `delete`, one in ask would prompt for a read, and the same applies to `drains`, `devices`, `browser`, `features`, `models` and `workflows`. The `ask` tier IS the single confirmation for the verbs that sit in it — /lua-workflow, /lua-drains, /lua-devices, /lua-decisions, /lua-browser, /lua-env and /lua-integrations rely on that prompt and do not ask a question of their own on top. NOTES ON INDIVIDUAL ROWS. `lua sync`: the guarded directions are allowed (the CLI's conflict guard refuses a pull that would overwrite local changes) and `--force`, which switches the guard off, asks; both spellings are listed because lua-cli 3.58.0 documents `--pull` and keeps `--accept` as its alias. `lua env *` asks even for `--list`, since the CLI prints masked values. `lua logs export` asks in both spellings (`--ci` binds anywhere, so `lua logs --ci export` would otherwise ride the `lua logs --ci*` allow): an export is org-wide and can include message bodies. `lua push * --ci --force*` is allowed because a push only stages a version — except for the types that have no version to gate: `lua push device`, `lua push device-trigger` and `lua push browser` sit in ask ABOVE that allow, because a pushed device is live on the agent's next turn and a pushed browser rewrites the live profile's policy. `lua devices credential` additionally needs `--out <file>`: without it the secret is printed into the conversation. `lua browser read` is allowed (one cloud session, prints the page, changes nothing) while `lua browser run` asks: a run clicks, types and can submit on a real third-party site, spends up to `--max-cost` of model budget, and with `--login` acts as the person there. `lua decisions run` is allowed for the same reason a read is: one billed call that changes nothing. Log-drain secrets never reach a command line — a header value is prompted or read from an env var (`--header-from-env NAME=ENV_VAR`) and the signing secret is minted server-side and printed once — so there is no credential-printing drain rule to deny. MCP: the read-only `lua-platform` server is allowed as a whole (all five of its tools are GET-only), while the remote `lua-docs` and `ui` servers are allowed tool by tool and never as a whole server, because a remote host can add tools at any time and a whole-server rule would pre-approve them unseen; `submit_feedback` on the docs server is deliberately not pre-approved. Both the plugin-qualified and the bare spelling of each name is listed, since the bare one covers a server the user registered themselves.
